segments.heading: Machine state checks, continued: the boot with 10 modules
segments.text:
These lines are top-level statements. They continue the raw-file checks for the machine state section of the page, which start at line 811.
- `k-1.txt` is the saved kernel log of the boot BASEd10. `K10_LINE` holds the numbers of its lines with the text `This system has 10 DIMM sockets`.
- The script stops unless exactly one such line exists and line 1 starts with `Nov`, a day and a time.
- `BOOT10_FROM` is the date and time of line 1 of that log. The year 2026 and the month 11 are fixed text of the script. In the saved output of a build it is 2026-11-17 04:17:19 [Ref5].
The comment gives the purpose. The number in this Linux kernel line is not the number of slots of the board: this boot printed 10, and the boot of the rerun printed 12 (checked in line 897).

segments.heading: Function `mem_line`: the memory size line of a kernel log
segments.text: Takes the lines of a kernel log. It searches each line for the text `kernel: Memory: <a>K/<b>K available`. It stops unless exactly one line matches. It returns the line number and the number `<b>` (the second number, after the slash) as an integer.

`k10` holds the lines of `k-1.txt`. `kl` holds the lines of `k-5.txt`, the saved kernel log of the 8000 MT/s boot (line 934).
- `MEM_LESS_GIB` is the difference of the two numbers after the slash, divided by 1024 x 1024.
- The numbers are in KiB (1 KiB = 1024 bytes), so the result is in GiB (1 GiB = 1024 x 1024 KiB).
- The script stops unless the result is exactly 64 GiB.
- `k-5.txt` holds 402090256K and `k-1.txt` holds 334981392K, so the difference is 67108864 KiB.

`dmi17-7200.txt` is the module list that was saved in the boot of the rerun.
- `DMI_N` counts the lines that are exactly `Memory Device` (one per module).
- The script stops unless `DMI_N` is 12, 12 lines hold the text `Configured Memory Speed:`, and 12 lines are exactly `Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`.
- Line 1165 reads the modification time of the file as a UTC time of day. The script stops unless it equals `BOOT_LAST`, the end time of row 0 of `boots.txt` (line 907). The message says `not inside row 0`, but the test is equality with that end time.

Line 6 of `try6.txt` reads `modules=24` in the saved data. `TRY6_MODLINE` is that number (line 900). The comment says that it is not the module count. These lines test that it is the number of lines with `Size: 32 GB` in the module list, two per module.
- `DMI_SIZE` counts the lines of the module list that contain `Size: 32 GB`.
- `DMI_SIZE_PLAIN` counts the lines that are exactly `Size: 32 GB`. `DMI_SIZE_VOL` counts the lines that are exactly `Volatile Size: 32 GB`.
- The script stops unless `DMI_SIZE` equals `TRY6_MODLINE` and the sum of the two exact counts, and each exact count equals `DMI_N`.
- The saved output of a build shows 24 lines: 12 `Size` lines and 12 `Volatile Size` lines [Ref5].
`check(True, ...)` adds one line to the self-check list. It holds the values that lines 1140 to 1171 checked. The line is always PASS: a false fact has already stopped the script in a `need` call.

`gl` and `g2l` are the lines of the two run logs (line 873). The script stops unless every line that starts with `done ` continues with `/home/jhan/`. So every result folder that the logs name lies under the home folder of the user jhan.

segments.heading: Argument lines: which process ran which line
segments.text: The block up to line 1231 answers two questions from the raw files. Which earlier rows ran the argument line of part L? Did the argument lines of part C run before the rerun?

segments.heading: Function `spec_line`: the argument line of a spec file
segments.text:
Reads a spec file and drops its empty lines.
- It stops unless exactly one line is left and that line contains `|`.
- It splits the line at the first `|` into the name and the arguments.
- It returns the name, the arguments without spaces at both ends, and the kernel sequence (the word after `--seq`).
- It stops when the arguments hold no `--seq`.

segments.heading: Function `launch_args`: the arguments of a launch line
segments.text:
`folder` is a result folder in the short form `R/...`. `tag` is the name of a process.
- The function reads `launches.txt` of that folder and takes the lines that start with `launch <tag> `.
- It stops unless exactly one such line exists and holds the text ` args `.
- It returns the text after ` args `.
- The runner script `rx.sh` writes such a line directly before it starts the binary with these arguments.

`SPEC` maps `like`, `cfwd` and `crev` to the result of `spec_line` for the spec file of that name in `S`.
- `LINE_L` is the name of the part L line. In the saved data it is `a6456`, and the csv file of such a process is `a6456.csv`.
- The lambda `no_seq` replaces the kernel sequence of an argument line by `X`.

The script stops unless the three argument lines are equal after this replacement and the three kernel sequences are three different texts. So the argument lines of part L and of part C differ in the kernel sequence only.
- Before the sequence all three files hold `--threads 120 --cpus 0-63,64-119 --bytes 256M --stop common --start common --min-ms 6000 --rounds 2`.
- After the sequence all three hold `--count --pmu-type 11 --events` and the same list of 6 events. `--count` makes the runner count hardware events of the CPU.

`SAME_LINE_FOLDERS` is the sorted list of the result folders of the `oldread` records of part L, control I, F72d12 and row L-1. The script stops unless the list has 7 folders and the launch line of the process `LINE_L` in each folder holds exactly the arguments of `like.spec`. Line 1203 stops the script unless the csv file of each of these records is `LINE_L` plus `.csv`. So these rows ran the same benchmark arguments as part L.

`C_FOLDERS` is the sorted list of the result folders of the `oldread` records of part C. For each folder the script takes the csv file names of these records, without `.csv`. It stops unless the folder has one name, the name is `cfwd` or `crev`, and the launch line of that process holds exactly the arguments of the spec file with the same name.

A scan of every csv file under the results folder `R`, at any depth. `N_CSV` counts the files. The scan uses header lines only. It takes no rate from these files.
- Only the lines that start with `# bwx` are used.
- A line of the form `# bwx<digits> trial mode:` is skipped. The comment says that such files are one-CPU trial files of older runners and hold no kernel sequence.
- Read again for this companion: 43 csv files hold such lines. All 43 lie in folders whose names start with `bwx8-`, `bwx9-`, `bwx10-` or `bwx11-`. None of these files holds a `# bwx: seq=` line.
- 37 of the 43 files hold process header lines. Each of these lines holds `--trial` and one CPU number. The other 6 files hold no process header line.

The lines that start with `# bwx` and are not skipped:
- Each one must start with `# bwx: seq=`. If not, the script stops.
- `fo_` is the top-level result folder of the file, in the form `R/...`.
- `SEQ_FOLDERS` maps each kernel sequence to the set of folders with a file that holds it.
- `READ_FOLDERS` collects the folders with a sequence that names the kernel `read`. The sequence is split at its commas, so the names `oldread` and `asmread` do not count.

Three hard assertions on the result of the scan follow (lines 1224, 1227 and 1229), then one line for the self-check list. Line 1224: the folders with the sequence of `cfwd.spec` or of `crev.spec` must be exactly the part C folders. So no csv file in another folder under `R` holds a part C sequence.
`READ_OTHER` lists the folders with the kernel `read` in a sequence that are not part C folders. The comment calls them folders of the older runner bwx.

The script stops unless both hold:
- The list `READ_OTHER` is not empty.
- Each name starts with `R/B5-`, `R/B7-`, `R/C3-` or `R/SHORT-` and a date of 2026-11-13 or 2026-11-14.
The script tests the folder names only. Read again for this companion:
- Every process header line of the 7 folders names the binary `bwx`, except 3 lines of the `SHORT` folder. These 3 lines name `bwx_o0`, `bwx_o36` and `bwx_o52`.
- The kernel sequences of these 3 lines do not hold `read`. So each of the 124 process header lines with `read` in its sequence names the binary `bwx`.
Every folder of the records in `OTHER` must be in `READ_OTHER`. If not, the script stops.

The `check` call adds one PASS line with the counts. The rules file states that no earlier bwx12 result at 8000 MT/s holds the kernel `read`. This scan tests that statement on the header lines. The saved output of a build shows 903 csv files, 4 part C folders and 7 folders in `READ_OTHER` [Ref5].

segments.heading: Function `bwx_header`: header lines of a bwx process
segments.text:
Takes one record of the older runner bwx and checks the header lines of its process in the csv file. Rule V2 point 4 asks the report to state how these rows differ from part C (comment in lines 1233 and 1234). Table 6 of the page gives their load at launch.
- From the I row of the record the function goes back line by line to the nearest line that starts with `-- ` (the process header line).
- That line must hold the tag of the record, the binary `bwx`, the launch time of the record and its 1-minute load average at launch. If not, the script stops.

The second half of `bwx_header`. The script stops unless both hold:
- Exactly one `# bwx:` line lies between the process header line and the I row. Its `start=` and `count=` values equal the fields `start` and `count` of the record. The arguments of the header line hold `--start` with the same value.
- The arguments hold a kernel sequence (`--seq`).
It returns the line number of the header line, the start option, the counter setting and the sequence. It adds the dataset, the tag, the launch time and the load of the record.

`X_HEAD` gets one `bwx_header` result per process of `OTHER` (one per `proc_key`). The call uses the first record of the process in the list. `X_POOL_HEAD` holds the processes of the datasets B7a, B7b, C3a and C3b (`BWX_POOL`, line 322). `X_REV_HEAD` holds the others.

The script stops unless all of these hold:
- `X_POOL_HEAD` has 24 processes and `X_REV_HEAD` has 4.
- The counter setting is 0 in every process of B7a and B7b, and 1 in every process of C3a and C3b.
- Each of the four datasets has records, and its first folder name starts with `R/B7-`, `R/B7-`, `R/C3-`, `R/C3-`, in this order. The operator `:=` stores the folder lists in `X_FILES_` inside the expression.
- `X_OFFSET` is 12. It counts the processes of the 24 with the start option `offset`. The others have `common`. A process has `offset` exactly when its tag contains `-offset-`.

The same two settings for part C. For each part C folder the script takes the csv file of the first `oldread` record. It stops unless the file has exactly one `# bwx:` line, with `start=common` and `count=1`, and the launch line of the process holds `--start common` and the word `--count`. Line 1275 stops the script unless every part C record of `oldread`, `read` and `asmread` has `count` 1 and `start` `common`.

`X_SEQ` is the kernel sequence of the 24 processes.
- The script stops unless all 24 header lines hold the same sequence.
- Then the sequence is split at its commas.
- The script stops unless it has 8 kernels, its first three are the sequence of `cfwd.spec` (oldread, read, asmread) and its last three are the sequence of `crev.spec` (asmread, read, oldread).
- So in these rows `read` at position 1 ran directly after `oldread`, and `read` at position 6 ran directly after `asmread`.
- The `check` call adds one PASS line with these counts.

segments.heading: X2d12 and the three boots with 10 modules
segments.text:
The rules file quotes four more processes that are not rows of the list of 8000 MT/s rows. Each one ran the argument line of part L once on 2026-11-17, in a boot of its own: X2d12 with 12 modules, and X1d10, X1d10b and BASEd10 with 10 modules.
- The lines up to 1344 check them in the raw files and compute their rates.
- The page shows these rates in notes under Table 2.
- No wording of the page comes from them.

segments.heading: Function `klog_boot`: times and module count of a kernel log
segments.text:
Reads the saved kernel log `<name>.txt` of the folder `dimm-check-20261117`.
- It takes the time of day of the first and of the last line. Both lines must start with `Nov 17`.
- It collects the lines of the form `This system has N DIMM sockets`.
- It stops unless both times are found and exactly one such line exists.
- It returns the path, the two times (`t0`, `t1`), the number N (`modules`), the number of that line (`line`) and the number of lines of the file (`last`).

The loop runs once per row: X1d10 (log `k-4`), X1d10b (`k-3`), X2d12 (`k-2`), BASEd10 (`k-1`).
- `o_` and `a_` are the records of the dataset with `oldread` at position 0 and with `asmread` at position 1. `expect` stops unless each group has 2 intervals of 1 process with 120 threads. Other records are left out: in facts.json the dataset X2d12 also holds 6 records of read_nop96, read_nop256 and read_1pl.
- `kb` holds the facts of the kernel log from `klog_boot`. `fo` is the result folder of the first `oldread` record.
- Lines 1 and 2 of `launches.txt` must be the `launch` line and the `rc 0` line of the process `LINE_L`.

More hard assertions inside the loop. Lines 1308 to 1311:
- Every record must name the folder `fo` and the file `LINE_L` plus `.csv`.
- It must be a bwx12 record at 8000 MT/s with the common stop and 6000 ms intervals.
- Its module count must be the count of the kernel log.
- Its launch time and load must be those of the `launch` line.
- Both groups must come from one process, and each `asmread` interval must follow `oldread` directly.
Line 1312: the launch line must hold exactly the arguments of `like.spec`.

The last hard assertions inside the loop.
- Line 1313: launch and end of the process must lie between the first and the last line of the kernel log. The log must start after `BOOT8_TO` (line 937), the time of the last line of the saved kernel log of the 8000 MT/s boot. `BOOT8_TO` must be a time of 2026-11-17.
- Lines 1315 and 1316: the records of a row must name one boot.
- Line 1317: `EXTRA` then keeps both groups, the log facts, the folder, the launch time, the end time, the load and the boot.

More hard assertions on the four rows.
- Line 1318: the four boots and the boot of the used 8000 MT/s records (`EIGHT`, line 310) are 5 different boots.
- Line 1319: the four kernel logs do not overlap in time. Their order is X1d10, X1d10b, X2d12, BASEd10.
- Line 1320: the module counts of the four logs are 10, 10, 12 and 10.

More hard assertions. They test the order in time of the four boots and of the recorded changes of the firmware settings. Lines 1322 to 1324 compare the first log line of each boot with `X1_T`, `X2_T` and `RV_T` (lines 1064 to 1066). These are the times in line 1 of the three files `set.txt` of the TXREQ changes.
- X1d10 and X1d10b started after the change of TXREQ Min and before the change of TXREQ Max.
- X2d12 started after both changes, and its process ended before both settings were changed to their original values again (`RV_T`).
- BASEd10 started after that.
- Line 1325: all four logs end before `D72_T` (line 1092), the file time of the settings file that changes DIMM Frequency to 7200 MT/s. Only the times of day are compared, not the dates. Read again for this companion: the date of this file time is 2026-11-17.

Lines 1326 to 1330 compute rates of the four rows.
- The rows hold 16 records, and 14 of them get a rate. No line of the script computes a rate for the 2 `asmread` records of BASEd10.
- Each `Rg` call computes the rate of its records with `val` (line 176): the sum of `bytes / elapsed_s / 1e9` over the 120 T rows after the I row.
- `val` stops the script unless this sum, rounded to 0.001 GB/s, equals the field `GBps` of the record.
- The script does not compare these 14 rates with the rate that the I row prints: the test of lines 341 to 345 covers only `USED` and `OTHER`. Computed again for this companion: each of the 14 sums, rounded to 0.01 GB/s, equals the printed rate or lies 0.01 GB/s above it.
`rX2_old` and `rX2_asm` are the ranges of the 2 `oldread` intervals and of the 2 `asmread` intervals of X2d12.

The values of the boots with 10 modules:
- `T10_ASM`: the `asmread` ranges of X1d10 and of X1d10b, 2 intervals each. The median of 2 values is their mean. Rule V1 point 3 quotes these two boots as two boots at equal settings.
- BASEd10 is not in `T10_ASM`. It started after the revert (line 1324), so its recorded firmware settings differ from those of the two boots.
- `T10_APART`: the higher of these two medians divided by the lower one, minus 1, times 100. It is the distance of the two medians in percent of the lower median.
- `rT10_old`: the range of the `oldread` intervals of the three boots with 10 modules. The script stops unless it has 6 intervals of 3 processes.
Computed again for this companion: the two medians are 261.52 and 286.01 GB/s, which gives 9.4 %.

Cross-checks of these values with `FACTS.md`. `g0` is the length of the self-check list before them. Lines 1332 and 1333: the two ranges of X2d12 against the cell `Min to max, GB/s` of the X2d12 row in sections 4.2 and 4.4, each end to 0.01 GB/s. A missing X2d12 row stops the script in `facts_row`.

Lines 1334 to 1337: section 4.6 must hold a sentence of the form `gave asmread a / b and c / d GB/s, e % apart`. The four `asmread` values (rounded to 0.01 GB/s) and `T10_APART` (rounded to 0.1 %) are compared with it. A sentence that is missing in section 4.6 gives a FAIL line.

- Lines 1338 to 1341: section 4.6 must hold the sentence on the old read range of the three 10-module boots, with the same n. Both ends (0.01 GB/s) and the width in percent of the lower end (`width_pct`, rounded to 0.1 %) are compared. A sentence that is missing in section 4.6 gives a FAIL line.
- Line 1342: `grouped` replaces the 4 checks of lines 1332 to 1341 by one line of the self-check list.
- In each of the 4 checks, a comparison passes when the two values differ by at most one rounding step, 0.01 GB/s or 0.1 % (`near`, line 616).
The `check` call adds one PASS line that summarises lines 1299 to 1325.

Lines 1346 to 1348 search `FACTS.md` for the list with the title `Decisions made while this sheet was built, after the numbers were seen:`. The script stops unless this list has the items `(k) Range of the 8000 MT/s side` and `(r) Part C against 8000 MT/s`. The page follows both decisions.
- Decision (k) takes the pool of rows L-1 to L-4 as the 8000 MT/s range for parts L and C.
- Decision (r) gives a comparison with 8000 MT/s rows for two rows of part C (`oldread`, and `asmread` directly after `oldread`), although rule F2 says to show part C at 7200 MT/s only.

segments.heading: One-thread phase of 2026-11-13 and rule F1 point 5
segments.text:
`one-thread.csv` lies in the result folder of row A-1. Line 1352 stops the script when row A-1 is in another folder.
- `one_h` holds the process header lines of the file (lines that start with `-- `). `one_t` holds the launch time at the end of each line.
- The script stops unless every header line has a launch time and holds the text ` threads 1 `.
- `ONE_N` is the number of these processes. `ONE_FIRST` and `ONE_LAST` are the first and the last launch time.
- Line 1357: no launch time may be earlier than the one before it. The first 120-thread process of row A-1 (`A1_FIRST`, line 991) must start 0 s to 1 s after the last one-thread launch.
The saved output of a build shows 192 one-thread processes from 18:12:23 to 18:17:20 and the first 120-thread launch at 18:17:21 [Ref5].

Rule F1 point 5 needs the rate of the old read kernel after one-thread work and directly after 120-thread work. `rA12_old` is the range of the bw_old read records of rows A-1 and A-2. `expect` stops unless they are 12 intervals of 4 processes. The rates are the `GBps` fields of these part A records.

The loop tests the order of the processes in the csv files of rows A-1 and A-2.
- `HA1` and `HA2` are the process header lines of the two csv files (line 990). `_fproc` is the number of the process of a record inside its csv file (line 349).
- Line 1365: in each file the round-1 process of bw_old read must be process 1, and the round-2 process must be the last process.
- Line 1367: the process before the last one must be a 120-thread process of bw_new with the kernel `read`.
- `A12_GAP` gets the seconds between the launches of these last two processes. Line 1370 stops the script unless each gap is above 0 s and at most 5 s. The saved output shows 2 s and 3 s [Ref5].

Row A-2 started after one-thread work too. `ONE2` is the result folder of the run before it. The script stops unless all of these hold:
- Every process header line of `A5.csv` and `A6.csv` holds the text ` --threads 1 `.
- `launches.txt` of the folder has as many lines that start with `== ` as there are header lines.
- `A5.csv` and `A6.csv` are the only csv files of the folder.
- `env.txt` holds exactly one line `## end utc=...`, and the first launch of row A-2 (`A2_FIRST`, line 991) is more than 0 s and at most 10 s after that time.

`xc_text_range` adds a check: the range of `rA12_old`, rounded to 0.01 GB/s, must be present in section 1.5 of `FACTS.md` in the form `low to high`. The last `check` adds a PASS line with the range, n and the gaps. The saved output shows 464.42 to 467.06 GB/s from 12 intervals of 4 processes [Ref5].

The earlier report (`EARLIER`, line 32) must exist, and its text must hold the words `the rule inside the core that causes this is not established`. If not, the script stops. The reference list of the page says that the Short version of that report holds this statement (line 1455). The raw-file checks that started at line 811 end here.

segments.heading: Reference list of the page
segments.text: `addref` (line 815) adds one entry to `REFS`: a key, the path in short form and a note. It stops when the path does not exist. All `addref` calls of the file are in lines 1389 to 1474. These lines add the facts sheet, `facts.json` and the rules file.

The note of the key `gen` (the reference to this script) gives the reason for the sum in `val`. The records hold each bwx rate rounded to 0.001 GB/s. A second rounding to 0.01 GB/s can change the last digit. So the script sums the 120 thread rows and rounds once.
References to `build_facts.py`, to the scripts `go.sh`, `ra.sh` and `go2.sh`, to the three spec files and to the two run logs.

References to the csv files of the rerun, one per step: part A (sessions 1 to 3, `threads120.csv`), part L (sessions 1 to 3, `a6456.csv`), part C (T72C1 to T72C4) and control I (T72I1, T72I2).
- Each path comes from the field `folder` of the first old-kernel record of that session or tag.
- For part C and control I the file name comes from the field `file`.
- Then follow the files of F72d12 (csv file, `launches.txt`, `env.txt`), `gaps.txt`, and the `env.txt` files of part L and control I (`VISIT_ENV`, line 1128).
- No rate is computed here.

References to the 8000 MT/s rows. Rows A-1, A-2 and A-3: the csv files, with the line numbers of the header lines that the checks above used. Then the csv file and `launches.txt` of row L-1, and the csv file of process p1nop of row L-2.

The reference to the csv file of process p2add of row L-2. Its note holds two rates of the lowest `asmread` interval of the pool (`LOWEST_ASM`, line 520). The two rates use different formulas.
- `i_row_rate` returns the rate that its I row prints. The I row divides the total bytes of the 120 threads by the longest elapsed time of a thread. Line 1 of the csv file states this formula.
- `val` returns the sum of its 120 T rows. It divides the bytes of each thread by the elapsed time of that thread and adds the 120 results.
- `f2` rounds both to 0.01 GB/s.
- Read again for this companion from the csv file of process p2add: the I row prints 288.53 GB/s, and the sum is 288.540691 GB/s. So the page shows 288.54 GB/s for this interval.
References to `launches.txt` of row L-2, and to the csv files and `launches.txt` of rows L-3 and L-4.

References to the raw files of the machine state checks: `try6.txt`, the module list, `boots.txt`, the journal lines and the kernel log of the 8000 MT/s boot, the kernel log `k-1.txt` of the boot BASEd10 (10 modules), the firmware settings files, the earlier report and `one-thread.csv`. Several entries hold line numbers that the checks computed. `addref` writes them in brackets after the path. Examples: the lines of the hardware error records (line 1444) and the memory size lines (lines 1446 and 1448).

References to the csv file, `launches.txt` and the kernel log of X2d12, and to the csv files and kernel logs of the boots with 10 modules. Line 1466 stops the script unless the kernel log of BASEd10 is the file `KLOG10` of line 1141. That file already has the key `klog10`.

References to the csv files of the older runner bwx.
- For each of the 6 datasets (B7a, B7b, C3a, C3b, B5a-rev, B5b-rev) the script takes the folder and the file of its records in `OTHER`.
- It stops unless each dataset has exactly one csv file and the 6 files are different.
- Line 1476 stops the script unless the two `-rev` datasets lie in other folders than the four pool datasets.
- It also stops unless the `read` records and the `asmread` records of the `-rev` datasets come from the same processes (`procs` of `Rg`).

segments.heading: Small HTML helpers
segments.text:
Two fixed labels. `CI` is the text for control I, and `F72` is the text for F72d12.
- A sentence of the page that uses a label says that control I was added after the first numbers were seen, or that F72d12 is not part of the rerun.
- Other places of the script write the same words directly.
- A check near the end of the file (from line 2794) tests every paragraph, list item, caption, tooltip, word definition and table row of the page. Each one that names control I or F72d12 must hold these words.

segments.heading: Function `strip_tags`: plain text of an HTML text
segments.text: Removes the reference marks (`span` elements of the class `ref`). Then it replaces every HTML tag by a space. Then it turns HTML character codes such as `&` back into characters. The page checks at the end of the file use it.

segments.heading: Function `P`: one paragraph
segments.text: Adds the text to `PROSE` (the text that counts for the word limit) and returns it as an HTML paragraph. With `cls` the paragraph gets that class name. `chr(34)` is the double quote character.

segments.heading: Function `UL`: one bullet list
segments.text: Adds the items to `PROSE` and returns them as an HTML bullet list.

segments.heading: Function `table`: HTML of one table
segments.text:
`WIDE` names the table classes with a least width of 900 px. For such a table the function first writes a hint to scroll sideways.
- `head` is the list of column titles. A title that starts with `#` marks a number column: the `#` is removed, and the cells get the class `n`. The style block aligns this class to the right (line 2606).
- A row that is a text becomes one title row over all columns (class `grp`).
- Any other row is a list of cells.
The function computes no value.

segments.heading: Function `small`: text in small type
segments.text: Wraps a text in a `span` element of the class `sm` (small type).

segments.heading: Function `T`: one SVG text element
segments.text: Line 1519 starts the code of figure 1, the dumbbell chart. `T` returns one SVG `text` element at the place `x`, `y`, with a font size, a colour, an alignment (`anchor`) and an optional weight. The text is escaped with `esc`.

Two attribute texts for `T`. `HALO` draws a 3.5 px wide outline in the background colour `SURF` under the letters. So a line behind a text does not cross the letters. `TAB` asks for digits of equal width.

segments.heading: Function `marker`: one dot of figure 1
segments.text:
Returns the SVG circle of one dot. `color` is the colour of the kernel: `fig1` passes blue for the old read kernel and orange for the load-only loop (line 1669).
- A hollow dot (an 8000 MT/s row) has the background colour inside and an outline of 2.2 px in the kernel colour.
- A filled dot (a 7200 MT/s row) is a circle in the kernel colour on a larger circle in the background colour.
- The classes `ho` and `fi` tell the style block which kind of dot it is. So the style for a dot under the pointer does not replace the outline of a hollow dot.

segments.heading: Function `kernel_name`: display name of a kernel
segments.text:
Uses the first record of the list only.
- Part A record: `bw_old read (old read kernel)` or `bw_new read (new read kernel)`, by the field `binary`.
- bwx record: `oldread (old read kernel)`, `read (new read kernel)` or `asmread (in place of the new read kernel)`, by the field `kernel`. Any other kernel name ends the script with a Python error (`KeyError`).

segments.heading: Function `dot_title`: tooltip of a dot of figure 1
segments.text: `rg` is an `Rg` object (line 192). The text gives the row name, the kernel, the median, every interval value, n as intervals and processes, and the source rows from `src` (line 359). `f2` rounds each rate here to 0.01 GB/s. The interval values are in the order of launch time and interval number, as `Rg` sorted them.

segments.heading: Function `f1_row`: one row of figure 1 as a dictionary
segments.text:
Returns a dictionary that holds its seven arguments under the same names.
- `old` and `new` are `Rg` objects: the old read kernel and the load-only loop.
- `drops` is a list of drops in percent.
- `hollow` is true for an 8000 MT/s row.
- `how` is a text that says how the drop was formed.

segments.heading: Function `bwx_row`: figure 1 row of one bwx12 process
segments.text:
`olds` and `news` are the old-kernel records and the load-only records of one row.
- `pairs_in_process` (line 407) pairs each load-only interval with the old-kernel interval of the same process and round.
- `old` is the range (`Rg`) of the old-kernel intervals of the pairs. `new` is the range of the load-only intervals.
- `drops_of` (line 421) gives one drop per pair: (1 - load-only rate / old rate) x 100. It uses the `val` values (6 decimals), not the rates rounded to 0.01 GB/s.
- A process with 2 rounds gives 2 pairs. The median of 2 intervals is their mean, so each dot of such a row is the mean of 2 intervals.
- Example, computed again for this companion: process T72C1 gave 466.013926 and 465.540271 GB/s for `oldread`, and 320.900964 and 320.888793 GB/s for `read`. The two drops are 31.14 % and 31.07 %. Both round to 31.1 %, so the figure prints one value, 31.1 %.

segments.heading: Rows of figure 1
segments.text:
`B1_8000` and `B1_7200` are the row lists of the first block of figure 1 (6 s intervals, runner bwx12). `IN_PLACE` is the note of the rows that use asmread in place of the new read kernel.
- `B1_8000`: one hollow row, L-1. Rows L-2 to L-4 are not rows of figure 1.
- F72d12: one row.
- Part L: one row per session, from the `oldread` records at position 0 and the `asmread` records at position 1 of that session.
- Part C: one row per process (T72C1 to T72C4), from its `oldread` records and its `read` records. The note names the kernel that ran directly before `read`. The `asmread` intervals of part C are not in figure 1.
- Control I: one row per process (T72I1, T72I2).
In a crev process (sequence asmread, read, oldread) the `oldread` interval of a pair ran after the `read` interval of the pair.

The row lists of the second block (0.5 s intervals, binaries bw_old and bw_new). `B2_8000` holds one hollow row per entry of `A8_PAIRS` (line 455): rows A-1 and A-2, rounds 1 and 2. That gives 4 rows. Row A-3 holds bw_old read only and is not in figure 1.

`B2_7200` holds one row per entry of `A_PAIRS` (line 451): sessions 1 to 3, rounds 1 and 2. That gives 6 rows. In each row of both lists:
- `old` and `new` are the ranges of the 3 intervals of the bw_old read process and of the bw_new read process.
- Each interval rate is the field `GBps` of the record: the column `aggregate_GBps` of its csv row, with 2 decimals. The header line of the csv file gives the formula of this column: the total bytes of all threads divided by the longest elapsed time of a thread [Ref3].
- The row has one drop, between the two medians: (1 - median of bw_new read / median of bw_old read) x 100 (`a_pair`, line 444).
The rows of the first block use another formula for a rate: the sum of the 120 thread rates (`val`, line 176).
`F1_BLOCKS` is the data of figure 1: two blocks, each with a group of 8000 MT/s rows and a group of 7200 MT/s rows. `lines` holds the block title in two lines for the narrow layout.

Two counts of the rows of figure 1, each with a hard assertion:
- `SAME_LINE_ROWS` holds the rows of `B1_7200` whose name does not start with `Part C`. They are the rows of the argument line of part L in the 7200 MT/s boot. The script stops unless there are 6.
- `F1_NROWS` is the number of all rows. The script stops unless it is 21 (1 + 10 + 4 + 6).

segments.heading: Function `fig1`: draws figure 1 as SVG
segments.text: `layout` selects one of three widths: `wide` (940 px), `mid` (726 px) or `narrow` (386 px). `W` is the width of the drawing. `X0` and `X1` are the x places of 0 GB/s and of 500 GB/s (`XMAX`). `sx` converts a rate in GB/s to an x place on this linear axis, which starts at 0.

The inner function `drawn` returns the note lines of a row. In the mid layout only, it breaks a note of more than 44 characters after its first comma. It stops the script when such a note has no comma.

Vertical places. No rate is used here. The loop goes through the blocks, groups and rows from top to bottom.
- It stores the `y` value of each one in its dictionary.
- A block also gets the height of its title bar (`th`), and a row gets its height (`h`).
- In the wide and the mid layout a row is 22 px high plus 13 px per note line.
- In the narrow layout a row is 52 px high plus 13 px per note line. The row name is drawn above the dots there.
- `H` is the height of the whole drawing.

Starts the SVG element. Its class (`f1w`, `f1m` or `f1n`) lets the style block show the one layout that fits the window. The loop draws a vertical grid line every 100 GB/s from 0 to 500 GB/s, with the number above and below it. The last lines write the unit `GB/s` and the axis title `Whole-chip read rate, GB/s. The axis starts at 0.`

Draws the grey title bar of each block, the title of each group, and the name and the note lines of each row. `cy` is the vertical place of the dots of a row. In the narrow layout the name is drawn above the dots, and a thin line is drawn under the row. No rate is used here.

Draws the measured values of one row.
- `xo` and `xn` are the x places of the median of the old read kernel and of the median of the load-only loop.
- `dt` is the drop text from `drop_txt` (line 425): the lowest and the highest drop of the row with 1 decimal, or one value when both are printed equal.
- Lines 1665 to 1668 draw the grey line between the two medians and write `dt` above its middle. The tooltip of the line gives the drop, how it was formed (`how`), the number of pairs and the source rows.

The loop of line 1669 runs once for the old read kernel (blue, number at the right) and once for the load-only loop (orange, number at the left).
- It draws the dot at the median with `marker`, and a thin bar from the lowest to the highest interval with a short vertical line at each end.
- It writes the median with 2 decimals (`f2`).
- Each dot has the tooltip of `dot_title` and an invisible circle of 12 px radius around it, which also shows the tooltip.
Lines 1677 and 1678 close the SVG element and return the drawing as one text. So figure 1 shows one median and one range per kernel and row. It shows no mean over rows and no total over rows.

segments.heading: Function `beeswarm`: vertical offsets of dots (figure 2)
segments.text:
Line 1681 starts the code of figure 2. `xs` holds the x places of the dots of one row.
- The function processes the dots from left to right.
- Each dot gets the first of five vertical offsets (0, -5.5, 5.5, -11, 11 px) in which no dot placed before lies closer than 8.6 px in x (2 x `r`).
- When no offset is free, the dot gets the last one, 11 px.
- The function returns the offsets in the order of `xs`.
- The offset changes only the vertical place of a dot. The rate of the dot stays on the horizontal axis.
- `panel` calls this function (line 1781) and stops the script when two dots lie 5.2 px or less apart (line 1786).
The next function, `p_row`, starts at line 1695.
